sections.section_name: Section B - Very Short Structural Functions

questions.question_text: Identify the primary source and the specific biological function of the immunosuppressive agent cyclosporin A used during human organ transplantation procedures. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: Cyclosporin A is produced by the fungus Trichoderma polysporum. It suppresses the recipient's cell-mediated immune response, specifically inhibiting T-cell activation to prevent the rejection of the transplanted organ.

questions.question_text: Define the biological concept of a 'selectable marker' and briefly state its indispensable role in the workflow of recombinant DNA technology. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: A selectable marker is a specific gene sequence (like antibiotic resistance) located on a vector. It allows researchers to selectively identify and isolate recombinant transformants while eliminating non-transformed host cells.

questions.question_text: Explain the ecological phenomenon of 'competitive release' observed in interacting biological communities when a dominant species is experimentally removed. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: Competitive release occurs when a competitively inferior species dramatically expands its geographic range or population size following the experimental removal or natural extinction of its dominant competing species.

questions.question_text: Differentiate strictly between active and passive immunity based on the origin of the functional antibodies involved in the host defense mechanism. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: Active immunity develops when the host's own immune system generates antibodies following exposure to an antigen. Passive immunity involves the direct administration of pre-formed antibodies (like anti-tetanus serum) for immediate defense.

questions.question_text: State the underlying principle and the key structural advantage of utilizing ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay) in the early detection of viral infections like HIV. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: ELISA relies on specific antigen-antibody interactions. Its extreme structural sensitivity allows the early detection of minute quantities of viral antigens or host antibodies long before physical disease symptoms appear.

questions.question_text: Trace the step-by-step life cycle pathway of the malaria parasite (Plasmodium) starting from the injection of sporozoites into the human bloodstream to the rupture of red blood cells. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: Infected mosquitoes inject sporozoites, which travel to the liver and multiply asexually. The resulting merozoites burst liver cells and infect erythrocytes. Inside RBCs, they multiply asexually again, eventually rupturing the cells to release toxins causing cyclic malarial chills.

questions.question_text: Describe the sequential biological and biochemical changes that occur in the aeration tanks during the secondary treatment pipeline of municipal sewage. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: Primary effluent is actively aerated, promoting vigorous growth of aerobic microbes into flocs. These microbes rapidly consume the major organic matter, drastically reducing the Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) of the effluent before it enters the settling tank.

questions.question_text: Outline the three fundamental thermal steps defining a single standard cycle of the Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) utilized for target DNA amplification. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: The cycle starts with Denaturation at $94^\circ\text{C}$ to separate DNA strands. Next, Annealing at $50-60^\circ\text{C}$ allows oligonucleotide primers to bind target sequences. Finally, Extension at $72^\circ\text{C}$ utilizes Taq polymerase to synthesize the complementary DNA strand.

questions.question_text: Explain the specific molecular mechanism by which the crystalline insecticidal protein (Cry protein) produced by Bacillus thuringiensis causes targeted lethality in susceptible insect larvae. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: The inactive protoxin is ingested by the insect larva. The alkaline pH of the insect midgut solubilizes and activates the toxin. Active Cry proteins bind to midgut epithelial cells, creating pores that cause cell swelling, lysis, and eventual death.

questions.question_text: Define the ecological terms 'Gross Primary Productivity' (GPP) and 'Net Primary Productivity' (NPP), and state the mathematical relationship connecting them in an ecosystem framework. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: GPP is the total rate of solar energy capture by producers during photosynthesis. NPP is the actual biomass available to consumers. They are related by the equation $NPP = GPP - R$, where R represents metabolic respiration losses.

questions.question_text: Describe the three primary causal factors contributing to the accelerated 'Sixth Extinction' event currently driving massive global biodiversity depletion. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: The primary drivers are severe habitat destruction and fragmentation due to urbanization, overexploitation of natural resources by humans, and the disruptive introduction of highly aggressive invasive alien species that outcompete native flora and fauna.

questions.question_text: Analyze the structural role of the 'Ti plasmid' in biotechnology, explaining how it is genetically modified to act as a safe cloning vector for higher plants. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: The Tumor-inducing (Ti) plasmid naturally transfers disease-causing T-DNA into plants. Biotechnologists disarm it by deleting the tumor-causing genes and replacing them with a target gene of interest, creating a harmless vector that still retains its efficient DNA delivery mechanism.

questions.question_text: Read the following ecological case context: A researcher maps the growth of a bacterial colony introduced into a sterile, closed-flask nutrient medium. The resulting population curve shows a slow initial lag phase, followed by an exponential log phase, before abruptly plateauing into a flat asymptote. Identify the mathematical model describing this specific growth pattern, explain the biological cause of the plateau, and state the governing differential equation. [40-50 words]
questions.answer: This scenario precisely describes the Logistic Growth Model. The population plateaus because essential nutrients in the closed flask become depleted, reaching the environment's fixed carrying capacity ($K$). The governing mathematical equation is $\frac{dN}{dt} = rN\left(\frac{K-N}{K}\right)$.

questions.question_text: Read the following biotechnological case context: A forensic lab utilizes gel electrophoresis to analyze DNA samples recovered from a crime scene. After running the agarose gel, the technician exposes it to UV radiation to visualize the separated fragments. Identify the specific chemical dye required to stain the DNA prior to UV exposure, explain the physical basis of the fragment separation along the gel, and describe the visible appearance of the bands. [40-50 words]
questions.answer: The gel must be stained with the intercalating dye Ethidium Bromide. Because DNA is negatively charged, fragments migrate toward the positive anode under an electric field, separating strictly by molecular size—smaller fragments travel faster and further. Under UV light, the DNA appears as distinct, glowing bright orange bands.

sections.section_name: Section E - Comprehensive Essays & Labeled Diagrams

questions.question_text: Detail the comprehensive molecular pathway of creating recombinant human insulin using E. coli host cells. Explain the genetic engineering strategy used by Eli Lilly in 1983 to overcome the structural barrier of the inactive pro-insulin precursor molecule. [50-60 words]
questions.answer: Human insulin is synthesized as an inactive pro-hormone containing an extra C-peptide, which bacteria cannot excise. Eli Lilly solved this by chemically synthesizing two separate DNA sequences coding strictly for the active insulin A and B chains. These were inserted into separate E. coli plasmids. The chains were extracted, purified, and chemically joined via disulfide bonds to yield functional mature insulin.

questions.question_text: Provide a detailed explanation of the human immune system's structural components involved in cell-mediated immunity. Outline how T-lymphocytes target, recognize, and destroy infected host cells, and explain this pathway's critical relevance to organ transplantation protocols. [50-60 words]
questions.answer: Cell-mediated immunity is driven by T-lymphocytes maturing in the thymus. Cytotoxic T-cells identify foreign or abnormal antigens presented on the surface of virus-infected or cancerous host cells. Upon recognition, they release perforins to induce targeted apoptosis. Because this system actively recognizes 'non-self' tissue grafts, it is the primary mechanism causing organ transplant rejection, necessitating lifelong immunosuppressive therapy.

questions.question_text: Describe the complete operational layout and biochemical process occurring within a standard biogas plant utilizing cattle dung. Trace the sequence of microbial actions starting from complex polymer breakdown to the final generation of methane gas, highlighting the role of methanogens. [50-60 words]
questions.answer: A biogas plant consists of a concrete tank fed with a dung-water slurry. First, facultative anaerobic microbes enzymatically hydrolyze complex polymers (cellulose/proteins) into simple monomers. Next, acidogenic bacteria convert these monomers into organic acids like acetic acid. Finally, strictly anaerobic methanogenic archaea (Methanobacterium) consume these acids and hydrogen to generate biogas—a combustible mixture predominantly composed of methane ($CH_4$), $CO_2$, and $H_2S$.
